title: Health & Fitness · Episode 1
chapters: Nutrition: what the evidence actually says

units.t: Health & Fitness. Episode one.
In this episode: What exercise does for you, Cardio fitness, Strength training and Nutrition: what the evidence actually says.
Part one. What exercise does for you.
If exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world.
You need less than you might think.
Closest to a wonder drug.
Regular physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers including bowel and breast cancer, depression, anxiety and dementia.
It strengthens bones and muscles, improves sleep and helps manage weight and blood pressure.
Researchers often say that if exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world.
The mind benefits too.
A 2024 review in the BMJ found that walking, jogging, yoga and strength training were effective treatments for depression, especially at higher intensity.
Exercise also boosts attention and memory, partly through more blood flow and growth factors in the brain.
It complements professional care; talk to your GP if you're struggling.
Every bit counts.
You don't need a gym session for movement to count.
The World Health Organization dropped its old rule that activity only counts in blocks of ten minutes in 2020, because the evidence showed every bit helps.
A 2022 University of Sydney study tracked more than 25,000 UK adults who didn't exercise.
Those who did three or four short bursts of vigorous activity a day, like charging up stairs or running for the bus, had up to 40% lower risk of early death.
It was observational, so it can't prove cause.
To judge effort, use the talk test.
Moderate: you can talk but not sing.
Vigorous: only a few words.
One minute of vigorous activity is worth about two of moderate.
Two exercise myths.
Can you outrun a bad diet?
Not easily.

In 2012, anthropologist Herman Pontzer found that the Hadza, hunter-gatherers in Tanzania who walk and work physically all day, burned about the same calories as office workers in Europe and the US, once body size was accounted for.
He argues the body trims energy spent elsewhere, and many people eat more after exercise.
So diet usually matters more for weight, though activity helps keep weight off and improves fitness, blood pressure, blood sugar and mood at any size.
The 10,000-step target traces to a 1960s Japanese pedometer, the manpo-kei, '10,000-step meter'.
Benefits begin well below it: about 7,000 steps is linked to far lower risk of early death than 2,000, with gains flattening beyond that.
Sitting less.
Many of us sit for most of the day: commuting, working and relaxing.
Long, uninterrupted sitting is linked with poorer health, somewhat independently of how much you exercise.
The guidelines recommend minimising prolonged sitting and breaking it up as often as possible.
Simple habits help.
Stand for phone calls, take the stairs, or walk to talk to a colleague instead of emailing.
Set a reminder to get up every 30 to 60 minutes, or use a standing desk for part of the day.
Making it stick.
The best exercise is the one you'll actually do.
Choose activities you enjoy, whether that's walking with a podcast, dancing, swimming, gardening, a team sport or lifting weights.
Start small, even ten minutes a day, and build gradually to avoid injury and burnout.
Schedule it like an appointment.
Exercising with a friend or group makes you more likely to turn up, and exercising outdoors or with others adds benefits from nature and social connection.
If you have a health condition or haven't exercised in a long time, check with your doctor first.
An accredited exercise physiologist can also help.
The key idea: Regular activity lowers the risk of many serious diseases and is an effective part of treating depression.
Part two. Cardio fitness.
Your heart is a muscle that answers to training.
How fit it is may say more about your future health than almost any other number.
Training your delivery system.
Cardiovascular exercise is any sustained activity that raises your heart rate and breathing: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, running, rowing, even vigorous gardening.
It trains a whole delivery system.
With regular training, the heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it can beat less often.
Muscles grow more tiny blood vessels, called capillaries, and more mitochondria, the structures inside cells that turn oxygen and fuel into energy.
That's why a trained person's resting heart rate is often lower.
A typical adult rests somewhere between 60 and 100 beats per minute, and many endurance athletes rest in the 40s or 50s.
Fitness and long life.
Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Australia, and regular aerobic exercise is one of the most reliable ways to reduce the risk.
It lowers blood pressure, improves cholesterol and makes the body more sensitive to insulin.
Active people also have lower rates of stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and some cancers, including bowel and breast.
Benefits start within a week or two.
VO2 max is the most oxygen your body can use in hard exercise.
Labs measure it with a mask; smartwatches estimate it.
Large observational studies link higher fitness with longer life, and low fitness carries a risk comparable to smoking.
VO2 max declines with age, but training slows the fall, and the biggest gains come when an inactive person starts moving.
Easy and hard effort.
Trackers divide effort into zones of your maximum heart rate.
A rough estimate of maximum is 220 minus your age, though real maximums vary by 10 or more beats.
Easy, conversational effort, zone 2, sits at about 60 to 70% of maximum.
Moderate intensity runs up to about 76%; vigorous is above.
Wrist readings can lag or jump, so many coaches also use a 0 to 10 effort scale, where zone 2 feels like a 3 or 4.
Many endurance coaches use polarised training: about 80% of sessions easy, 20% hard.
Hard intervals, such as four bouts of four minutes at high effort, raise fitness efficiently, and HIIT suits people short on time.
The best ratio is debated, but mostly easy with some hard is well supported.
The 2026 guidelines.
In March 2026, Australia replaced its physical activity guidelines with 24-hour movement guidelines covering activity, sitting and sleep.

Adults of all ages should do 30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity on most days, adding up to about two and a half hours a week, plus several hours of light activity, such as pottering around the house or garden.
For adults aged 18 to 64 who track their steps, the target is 7,000 or more a day.
Muscle strengthening on two or more days, and balance and mobility work on three or more, round out the week.
Starting safely.
For most people, moderate activity like walking is very safe, and the risks of staying inactive are far greater.
If you have a heart condition, chest pain, dizziness, unexplained breathlessness or other chronic health issues, speak with your GP first.
Exercise and Sports Science Australia publishes a short pre-exercise screening questionnaire.
Stop and seek medical help if you feel chest pain or pressure, severe breathlessness or faintness.
Begin with sessions you can finish comfortably and add a little each week.
The best cardio is what you keep doing: brisk walking, swimming, cycling, walking part of your commute, or parkrun, which welcomes walkers.
Tracking minutes rather than distance keeps beginners patient.
A GP or accredited exercise physiologist can tailor a plan.
The key idea: Cardio trains your heart, lungs, blood vessels and muscles to deliver and use oxygen more efficiently.
Part three. Strength training.
Muscle is not vanity.
It is what lets you climb stairs, carry shopping and get up off the floor at 85.
Strength at every age.
From around your 30s, you gradually lose muscle mass and strength unless you act, and the loss speeds up after about 60.
Severe age-related muscle loss is called sarcopenia.
It raises the risk of falls, fractures and losing independence.
Strength training is the most effective way to slow or reverse it.
It also improves blood sugar control, supports healthy bones and joints, and makes everyday tasks easier.
People in their 80s and 90s can still build meaningful strength with supervised training.
Grip strength, a simple measure of overall strength, is linked with longer life in large studies.
Muscles, bones and blood sugar.
Muscle and bone both respond to load.
When you lift something challenging, muscle fibres are stressed, then rebuild stronger.
Bones adapt to the forces placed on them too, which is why resistance and impact exercise help prevent osteoporosis.
An Australian trial at Griffith University, called LIFTMOR, found that carefully supervised heavy resistance and impact training improved bone density in postmenopausal women with low bone mass.
Muscle is also the body's biggest store for glucose from food, so more muscle helps keep blood sugar steady.
The metabolism boost is often overstated, though: each kilogram of muscle burns only slightly more energy at rest than fat.
Overload and compound lifts.
The core principle is progressive overload.
Your body adapts to the demands you place on it, then stops once a load feels easy.
To keep improving, add challenge gradually: a little weight, an extra rep or set, a slower movement, or less rest.
If you can do 10 good squats with a 10 kg dumbbell, aim for 12 next week, then move to 12 kg.
Muscles can grow across loads from about 6 to 30 repetitions, if sets finish close to fatigue.
Compound lifts give the most return: the squat, deadlift or hip hinge, bench press or push-up, overhead press, and row or pull-up.
Machines, dumbbells, bands and bodyweight all work.
Learn technique with light weights first, ideally with a qualified coach.
How often, and recovery.

Australia's 24-hour movement guidelines, updated in 2026, recommend muscle strengthening on at least two days a week for adults, plus balance and mobility work on three or more days, which matters most later in life for preventing falls.
Two full-body sessions of 30 to 45 minutes are enough for most beginners.
Start with one exercise per major movement pattern, two or three sets each, stopping with one to three reps in the tank.
Training is the stimulus; recovery is when you get stronger.
Many plans leave about 48 hours before hitting a muscle group hard again, and sleep matters because repair is active overnight.
Soreness a day or two later is normal and no measure of a good session.
Sharp, joint or persistent pain is worth checking with a physiotherapist or doctor.
Protein and myths.
Muscles are built from protein.
Australia's baseline is about 0.
84 grams per kilogram of body weight a day for men and 0.
75 for women, rising for people over 70.
For people who lift, benefits for muscle growth tend to level off near 1.
6 grams per kilogram.
A serve of 20 to 40 grams at each meal seems helpful.
Eggs, meat, fish, dairy, tofu, legumes and nuts all count; protein powder is convenient, not essential.
Several myths keep people out of the weights room.
Building large muscles takes years of deliberate training, so women won't get bulky by accident.
You can't burn fat from one spot, so crunches alone won't flatten a stomach.
Supervised strength training is safe for teens and doesn't stunt growth.
If you have a health condition, talk to your doctor first.
The key idea: Strength training slows age-related muscle loss and protects bone, blood sugar control and independence at every age.
Part four. Nutrition: what the evidence actually says.
Ignore the fads.
The science of eating well is simpler, and less exciting, than the internet suggests.
Cut through the noise.
One week coffee is bad for you, the next it's good.
Nutrition is genuinely hard to study.
We can't lock people in labs for decades, so much evidence is observational, showing links but not always causes.
Headlines amplify single small studies, and influencers sell fads.
Yet the big picture is steady.

The Australian Dietary Guidelines, based on a large review of evidence, recommend a wide variety from five groups: vegetables and legumes; fruit; mostly wholegrain grain foods; lean meats, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and legumes; and milk, yoghurt, cheese or alternatives.
Limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and sugars, and limit alcohol.
Drink plenty of water.
It's not glamorous, but it's backed by a mountain of evidence.
Vegetables and fibre.
Adults are advised five to six serves of vegetables and two of fruit a day.
A serve is about half a cup of cooked vegetables or a cup of salad.
Yet fewer than one in ten Australian adults eat enough vegetables.
Plant foods provide vitamins, minerals and beneficial plant compounds, and are linked with lower risks of heart disease, stroke and some cancers.
For most people, eating more of them is the single most useful change.
They also provide fibre, the part of plant food your body can't fully digest, which is why it helps.
Fibre keeps bowels regular, helps you feel full, slows sugar absorption and feeds gut bacteria.
Aim for about 25 grams a day for women and 30 for men.
Wholegrains, legumes, nuts and seeds are good sources.
Processed food and labels.
Ultra-processed foods are industrially made products, often with ingredients you wouldn't use at home, like flavour enhancers, emulsifiers and modified starches.
Think soft drinks, packaged snacks, confectionery and reconstituted meats.
They make up around 40% of the energy in the average Australian diet.
Large studies link high intakes with higher risks of obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and depression, though scientists still debate why.
On labels, compare similar products using the 'per 100 g' column, since serving sizes vary.
Ingredients are listed by weight, so sugar near the top means a lot, and it hides behind aliases like glucose syrup or dextrose.
One food Calorie is about 4.
2 kilojoules.
The Health Star Rating is a quick guide, but not perfect.
Myths worth dropping.
Some popular beliefs don't hold up.
'Detox' products are unnecessary, because your liver and kidneys do that job.
Most healthy people eating a varied diet don't need vitamin supplements, though some groups do, such as people who are pregnant or have specific deficiencies; ask a doctor.
There's no need to drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
Fluid needs vary, food provides some, and thirst is a reasonable guide for most healthy adults.
And no single 'superfood' transforms your health: patterns matter more than individual foods.
Make it sustainable.
The best eating pattern is one you can keep up.
Strict diets often fail because they're hard to sustain.
Small changes add up: add a vegetable to every meal, swap sugary drinks for water, choose wholegrain bread, keep fruit where you'll see it, cook at home a bit more.
Focusing on what to add, rather than only what to cut, tends to feel better and works well.
For personalised advice, especially with a health condition, an Accredited Practising Dietitian is the qualified professional to see.
The key idea: Nutrition headlines flip because the science is hard, but the big picture is stable: eat a variety of whole foods and limit saturated fat, salt and sugar.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did a 2024 review find about physical activity and depression?
Answer. Walking, jogging, yoga and strength training all helped.
Question two. Why is a trained person's resting heart rate often lower?
Answer. Each beat moves more blood, so fewer are needed.
Question three. Why does strength training matter as we get older?
Answer. It slows muscle loss and lowers fall risk.
Question four. Why do nutrition headlines so often contradict each other?
Answer. Much evidence is observational, and single small studies get amplified.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
